multimod

A unified framework for representing, transforming, and solving mathematical optimization models across languages and solvers.

multimod is an R package for representing, analyzing, transforming, and solving mathematical optimization models. It stores sets, mappings, parameters, variables, and equations in a structured abstract syntax tree (AST). Models can be constructed with R functions or imported from the supported subsets of GAMS and GNU MathProg.

The package validates and visualizes model structure, folds redundant dimensions, trims unused symbols, and stores models as JSON or in CSV- and Arrow-based workspaces. It renders models and equations as GAMS, GNU MathProg, JuMP, Pyomo, or LaTeX.

For continuous linear optimization, multimod can generate an LP matrix for HiGHS or cuOpt, write an MPS file, or run generated model code with the corresponding external toolchain. It also reads solver results into R.

multimod originated in energy system modeling and includes an energy model among its examples. Its model representation is not specific to that domain.

Architecture: from formulation to solution

A model can enter multimod through R constructors, supported equation syntax, or a supported source-code reader. Once represented as an AST, it can be inspected, reduced, saved, translated into another modeling language, or compiled directly into an LP matrix. Each output route operates on the same model representation.

┌─────────────────────────────┐
│        Model inputs         │
├─────────────────────────────┤
│ R constructors and DSL      │ → new_*(), ast_*(), mm_equation()
│ GAMS    (basic/linear only) │ → read_gams()
│ MathProg (limited features) │ → read_gmpl()
│ JuMP    (constraints only)  │ → mm_equation()
│ {{Pyomo, AMPL, MPS, ...}}   │ → {{...}}
└─────────────────────────────┘
              ↓
   ┌────────────────────────┐
   │   multimod Core        │        Analysis & Manipulation:
   │ (Abstract Syntax Tree) │         • fold_model()        [x]
   ├────────────────────────┤         • trim_model()        [x]
   │ • Sets & Aliases       │  →      • save_model()        [x]
   │ • Parameters           │         • as_visNetwork()     [x]
   │ • Variables            │  ←      • model statistics    [x]
   │ • Equations            │         • model_to_json()     [x]
   │ • Mappings             │         {{auto-mapping}}      [ ]
   └────────────────────────┘         {{symbolic simplify}} [ ]
                 ↓                                     ↓
┌──────────────────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
│ Output: model code               │  │ Output: LP matrix                │
├──────────────────────────────────┤  ├──────────────────────────────────┤

The diagram summarizes the architecture; the table under Capabilities lists the implemented functions.

The current tested scope is linear programming with continuous variables. Language importers cover documented subsets, and some output routes remain experimental; see Capabilities and the roadmap.

Native matrix route

For performance on large models, the matrix route includes a C++17 executor for supported equation plans. Enable it with options(multimod.engine = "native"); equations that cannot be lowered to a native plan continue through the R engine. The executor is multithreaded, slices large expansions, and is used by both model_to_lp() and the streamed MPS route.

write_mps(stream = TRUE) sends coefficient blocks to a native spool and MPS writer instead of materializing the complete sparse matrix in R. Its native scan, presolve-map, and remap steps can eliminate doubleton rows and proportional columns while the file is built. Build-time definition substitution is applied on the same route. These paths are intended to reduce matrix-build time and bound the memory used for coefficient blocks.

Large-model runs indicate that the native streamed route can substantially reduce matrix-construction and MPS-writing time relative to the earlier in-memory route. Performance depends on model structure and build options; detailed benchmarks will be reported separately.

Installation 

pak::pkg_install("optimal2050/multimod")

The matrix route requires the ‘highs’ R package. Other routes require their corresponding toolchains: glpsol (the ‘glpsol’ R package ships it), Julia with JuMP, or Python with Pyomo; see the “Configuring solver paths” article.

Quickstart: one model, several representations 

library(multimod)

toy <- example_models$toy          # built in R, see "Writing a model in R"
toy
#> Model: toy
#> Description: two-region capacity expansion toy model
#> Language:  multimod
#> Sets:  2
#> Mappings:  2
#> Aliases:  0
#> Parameters:  4
#> Variables:  3
#> Equations:  3

as_latex(toy$equations$eqDemand) |> cat()
#> \begin{flushleft}
#> \subsection*{\textbf{eqDemand} -- \textit{demand is met in every region}}
#> \quad$\textbf{eqDemand}
#> _{\texttt{region}}$
#> $\mid\left\{\texttt{region}\right\} \in \mathit{mR}_{\texttt{region}}$ \\
#> \begin{equation*}
#> \begin{adjustbox}{max width=\textwidth}
#> $\begin{aligned}
#> &\sum_{\texttt{tech}} \bm{\mathit{vGen}}_{\texttt{tech},\texttt{region}} \ge \mathsf{pDemand}_{\texttt{region}} \\
#> \end{aligned}$
#> \end{adjustbox}
#> \end{equation*}
#> \vspace{1em}
#> \end{flushleft}
as_gams(toy$equations$eqDemand) |> cat()
#> eqDemand[region]$mR[region]..
#>   sum(tech, vGen[tech,region]) =g=
#>   pDemand[region];

An equation is written as text — MathProg by default, GAMS or JuMP by choice — and parsed into the same tree the constructors build:

cap_total <- mm_equation(
  toy,
  "eqCapTotal: sum{t in tech, r in region} vCap[t,r] <= 2000",
  desc = "total installed capacity"
)
as_jump(cap_total, model = toy) |> cat()
#> @constraint(
#>     model,
#>     eqCapTotal,
#>     sum(vCap[(t, r)] for t in tech, r in region) <= 2000
#> )

The same model solved in R:

r <- solve_highs(toy, attach = FALSE)
r$objective
#> [1] 198000

or written for another toolchain and solved there:

ws <- tempfile("toy-"); dir.create(ws)
write_gmpl(toy, model_dir = ws);  solve_gmpl(toy, ws)$objective    # GLPK
write_jump(toy, model_dir = ws);  solve_jump(toy, ws)$objective    # Julia
write_pyomo(toy, model_dir = ws); solve_pyomo(toy, ws, load_results = TRUE)$objective

With the documented toolchains and example data, these routes return an objective value of 198000. The “Solving and reading results” article runs them side by side; “Two models from the field” does the same for the energyRt reference model and for OSeMOSYS, read from its MathProg source and solved both through JuMP and from the matrix.

Capabilities

Build a model in R new_set(), new_parameter(), new_variable(), new_equation(), the ast_*() expression constructors, validate(); mm_equation() for an equation written as MathProg, GAMS or JuMP text
Read a model read_gams() for the linear subset of GAMS; read_gmpl() for MathProg with data sections; mm_equation(lang = "jump") for a JuMP @constraint() statement
Render as_gams(), as_gmpl(), as_jump(), as_pyomo(), as_latex() for any node; write_gams(), write_gmpl(), write_jump(), write_pyomo(), write_latex() for the model
Solve in R model_to_lp(), solve_highs(), write_mps(), solve_mps(), check_matrix_numbers(), mm_session() for repeated solves
Solve through generated code solve_gmpl(), solve_jump(), solve_pyomo(), each loading the solution back
Reduce fold_model() drops dimensions a parameter does not vary over; trim_model() drops unused symbols
Store and exchange save_model(), load_model(), get_data() (CSV, Arrow IPC, Parquet); model_to_json(), ast_schema()

Linear programs with continuous variables are the tested class. Structural model reduction (fold_model(), trim_model()) is distinct from numerical solver presolving. GAMS output is readable but not yet runnable without edits, and there is no Pyomo reader; the roadmap lists what else is not done yet.

Development direction

The long-term architecture gives the native core Python and Julia interfaces beside the R one. Further research directions include AI-assisted formulation and support for nonlinear and stochastic optimization; these are planned, not implemented.

The repository is laid out for that architecture: the R package at the root, core/ holding the native core (copied into src/ for the R build) and python/ reserved for its Python binding, specs/ for the cross-language goldens, and one documentation site under docs/ with the R reference at /r/ beside the future language sections.

Integration with energyRt

energyRt uses multimod as its model compiler: energyRt::multimod_from_energyRt() builds the model from an interpolated scenario, and the LP or MPS multimod produces is what energyRt hands to a solver.
